episode_title: From Misnomer to Mentorship: Derrick Sier on Rebuilding Identity in Oklahoma City

segments.text: Welcome to Voices of OKC. We are back again this week. Thanks for joining us. We are so excited about where the podcast is headed. The kids are really getting engaged. We had a great episode.

That just dropped last week with Mayor Holt. Our student Jordan did a phenomenal job interviewing him. So I really appreciate everybody watching, listening, your support. It means a lot. These kids are gaining skills that are going to propel them into their adulthood, we believe, and that will help equip them for life in the future. So we're excited that you're a part of that. But today we're going to talk mentorship with one of the best in our city. Derrick Sier, thank you so much for joining us today, man. We are

We're excited to have you. You know, we've met here and there like really briefly in certain scenarios. Yeah, we never really had a chance to talk. And so just the time we've had before we were on camera, man, I really my head, my ears are sparking because I just love vision. I love what you guys are doing at Restore OKC, man. Just phenomenal work. But there is so much so much to Derrick. And so I can't wait to hear more about you, man. And I actually just want to start right here. You know, so what was life like growing up for you? Are you from Oklahoma City?
Oklahoma? What was that like, man? Absolutely. Born and raised in Tulsa, Oklahoma. Northside?

Northside, okay. Anybody that's familiar? Whenever people ask about the north side of Oklahoma City, I tell them, or north side of Tulsa, I tell them the east side of Oklahoma City, east side of St. Louis, south side of Chicago, south Dallas. Like, it's just one of those areas. And so very tight knit community.
Yeah. My dad, I drove buses. My mom was a school nurse. But one of the most important things that kind of shaped me in my youth was seeing my dad work with kids down at the park, Chamberlain Park.
Okay.
And he would drive kids back and forth and taught sports while he was down there, life skills, wash clothes, things like that.
And so that kind of formed and shaped me in the fire of North Tulsa. Went on to play football in Iowa.
Okay. College?
Yeah, college ball in Iowa. Moved back to...
At Iowa University?
No, no, no, no. It was a small school. Well, it's easier to say Iowa than say Graceland.
Sure. But college in general, play football, it's a different beast.
Oh, absolutely.
That's a huge accomplishment.
The game is faster and people are stronger.
Oh, yeah.
The commitment level is way more than I had in college.
And so moved back home, got married, got involved with Edmond Parks and Rec's Boys and Girls Club with Salvation Army.
Yeah.
Kind of did some community programming there.
Okay.
Led me to UCO where I did recreation management there.
Okay.
And got into corporate rec and then eventually launched my own team building mentoring company.
Oh, very cool. So how long have you been married?
I've been married 24 years, man.
24. You got me by the time.
I got you, man.
Yes, sir.

I'm going to say everything positive right now.
Yeah, here we go. There we go.

Yeah.
But yeah, it does knock off some edges of both of you.
Yeah.
Anyway, so yeah, very great for my wife and I'm sure you've outpunted your coverage as well.
Absolutely.
Yeah.
That's awesome, man. So your dad really had a big influence in your life as far as...
So that's a good question then that we can jump on.
So how important is it for the father to be in the home in regard to any young person's life?
Maybe not even in the home, but maybe just present.
Yeah, active.
He's available, active.
You know, what is that?
How important is that? And then I got another question to back that one up.
Yeah, absolutely. I know for the last 20, 25 years, I think there's been this misnomer of the absence of specifically black fathers in the lives of children.
And I think research, when they talk about fathers being in the home, they actually talk about residing within the four walls of the building.
Yeah.
But what we found out with a little more nuance is that while dads may not be in the home, they're still active and they're still present.
And so we were talking about birthdays, graduations, showing up for extracurricular activities, sporting events, being available for date nights.
They're active disciplinarians.
It's like then the numbers begin to change.
Sure.
And so I had the benefit of having a father that was not only in the home, but also meeting all of those things.
And so when I think about having a father specifically, I think it comes with a very specific flavor and nuance as it pertains to relationships and dynamics.
I could be very archaic and generalize the roles of mom and dad.
But I think when you boil it down, the dads have a very unique contribution as it pertains to the confidence, the identity of a child.
And so what I've learned by having my father in my life has been tremendous.
One of the things that my dad did also was not only was he present, but he brought other males into my life as well.
And some of those men had children.
Some of those men did not.
Some of those men were in the home with their children.
Some of those men were not.
And so what I got to see is not only what my experience taught me in that there are black men who are active,
but it was counterintuitive or counter like what was being said in the research.
Right.
And so it was there was something that I had to reconcile with what I was reading and hearing versus what I was seeing.
And so my dad being present, being in the home, introducing me to other people was very vital as it pertains to the formation of my identity,
not only as a black male, but also as an active father.
That's so good.
Yeah, I was I was glad you said that because I've I've ran across that same misnomer.
You know, it's very interesting.
There is a lot of very active, you know, black, white fathers that are active in their kids lives.
But specifically, I like to highlight that the black men in the community, because I think that was a major misnomer.
So I appreciate you highlighting that.
Absolutely.

Mm hmm.

And so what kind of impact can that have?
What's what kind of a game changer is that when a mentor can step into their life?
Yeah.

I love way.

We like to call him a master mentor.
He is a master mentor.
He not only has mentored way longer than I have, but he's mentored me as well.
Oh, I didn't know that.
Yeah.
And we talked about this.
Some research is taking place.
It's talking about the impact of positive adult influences outside of the home.
OK.
I'll say it again.
The impact of positive influences on children, adult figures outside of the home.
We're not talking about aunties, uncles.
We're not talking about mom, dad.
Unrelated.
Yeah.
Yeah.
We're talking about people outside of the home.
And we find that he did some research within Oklahoma City Public Schools, within a certain school, that showed children that had positive male figures in their lives that are outside of the home.
The more you had, the more the success, this affirmation, this positivity, this identity, that when you got to one, which means one plus family, that you saw a positive increase.
But when you got to two and three, that started to increase.
And so their high-performing, like their high-identity confirmation, like these students actively had six to ten additional positive adults in their life.
Yeah.

Yeah.
With each other.

It's the want, want, want, want, want, want.
Yep.

We didn't know anything going on.
So he must be valid.
So something validates it.
Yeah.

Okay.

Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.

Yeah.

So good.

a different perspective to arriving at the same point.
You know, it's interesting.

we're not necessarily in cahoots against them.

contributing to the wellbeing of this young person.

Yeah.

Gerald Scott.

he was one of the first people that I met.

City talking about mentorship.

Because he listened.
